questions.q: What does "unipolarity" mean in the context of the post-1991 international system, and which event marked its definitive onset?
questions.a: Unipolarity means a single state (the United States) possesses preponderant military, economic, and technological power with no peer competitor. The definitive onset was the disintegration of the USSR in December 1991, which ended the bipolar Cold War structure. A wrong answer (e.g., "unipolarity means US controls all countries" or "it began in 1945") reveals confusion between hegemony/empire and structural polarity, or inability to date the systemic shift.

questions.q: Explain why the European Union is considered an "alternative centre of power" despite not having a unified military or a single foreign policy.
questions.a: The EU is an alternative centre because its collective GDP (~$19.35 trillion, 2024) rivals the US, the euro challenges dollar dominance, its trade bloc status gives leverage in WTO disputes, and it wields normative power through conditionality (e.g., human rights clauses in trade agreements). A wrong answer focusing only on "no EU army" misses that power in contemporary world politics is multidimensional — economic, regulatory, and diplomatic power can constrain a military superpower without matching it tank-for-tank.

questions.q: A US multinational corporation wants to launch a new AI product in Europe. The EU's proposed AI Act classifies it as "high-risk" and imposes strict transparency and data-governance requirements. The corporation lobbies the US government to pressure the EU to weaken the rules. Applying the concept of "regulatory power" and "market power," explain why the EU can likely resist this pressure.
questions.a: The EU's single market of ~450 million affluent consumers gives it market power: the corporation cannot afford to exit. Its regulatory power (the "Brussels Effect") means its standards become global defaults because firms standardise to the strictest regime. The US government cannot easily retaliate without hurting its own firms' EU access. A wrong answer (e.g., "US will impose tariffs and win") ignores interdependence asymmetry and the EU's willingness to use trade defence instruments (anti-coercion instrument).

questions.q: Compare the "ASEAN Way" with the EU's integration model. Identify two structural reasons why ASEAN has not developed supranational institutions like the European Commission or European Court of Justice.
questions.a: (1) ASEAN's founding principle of non-interference and respect for national sovereignty (Bangkok Declaration, 1967) explicitly rejects supranational authority; the EU's founding treaties (Rome, Maastricht) progressively pooled sovereignty. (2) ASEAN's huge diversity in political systems (authoritarian, communist, democratic) and development levels makes consensus on binding rules harder than among relatively homogeneous European democracies. A wrong answer citing "ASEAN is younger" ignores that ASEAN (1967) predates the EU's Maastricht Treaty (1992) — the difference is design philosophy, not age.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "China's economic rise since 1978 has been the most significant constraint on US unipolarity." Support your judgment with three specific mechanisms linking China's economic integration to reduced American freedom of action.
questions.a: The claim is largely valid. Three mechanisms: (1) **Trade interdependence**: China is the largest trading partner for 120+ countries, including US allies (Japan, South Korea, Germany, ASEAN), making US decoupling costly for allies. (2) **Supply chain centrality**: US firms depend on Chinese manufacturing (electronics, pharmaceuticals, rare earths); tariffs hurt US consumers and firms. (3) **Institutional leverage**: China's WTO membership (2001) and leadership in AIIB, BRI, RCEP create parallel governance structures where US preferences can be outvoted. A wrong answer focusing only on "China's military growth" misses that economic integration preceded and enabled military modernisation, and that economic constraints on US policy are already operative while military parity is distant.

questions.q: Draft a 150-word policy brief for India's Ministry of External Affairs arguing whether India should deepen engagement with the EU, ASEAN, or China as a strategic counterweight to US unipolarity in the Indo-Pacific. Justify your choice using one economic and one diplomatic criterion.
questions.a: A strong answer selects **ASEAN** (or EU) with clear criteria. Example for ASEAN: Economic — ASEAN-India FTA (2010) and RCEP adjacency offer market access and supply-chain integration without China's asymmetry. Diplomatic — ASEAN centrality in ARF, EAS, ADMM-Plus gives India a platform to shape regional security architecture without binary US-China alignment. A poor answer picks China citing only "large market" while ignoring border disputes, trade deficit ($80B+), and strategic mistrust, or picks EU citing "shared democracy" while ignoring India's strategic autonomy concerns and EU's limited Indo-Pacific military presence. The brief must weigh trade-offs, not just list positives.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The "New World Order and Unipolarity after 1991" refers to the post-Cold War international system where the United States emerged as the sole superpower (unipolarity) following the ______ of the USSR, while alternative centres of power — primarily the European Union (EU), Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), and a rapidly rising China — began asserting economic and political influence to constrain unilateral American dominance and shape a multipolar trajectory.
Fill in the blank: Then trace three parallel stories: Europe building ______ institutions (EU), Southeast Asia crafting consensus-based cooperation (ASEAN), and China leveraging state-led capitalism.

Fill in the blank: The "New World Order and Unipolarity after ______" refers to the post-Cold War international system where the United States emerged as the sole superpower (unipolarity) following the disintegration of the USSR, while alternative centres of power — primarily the European Union (EU), Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), and a rapidly rising China — began asserting economic and political influence to constrain unilateral American dominance and shape a multipolar trajectory.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
